identification.summary: HURRICANE PANDA is CrowdStrike's name for a group it describes as likely of Chinese origin, reported in October 2014 using a 64-bit Windows privilege-escalation zero-day, CVE-2014-4113 [S1]. In April 2015 CrowdStrike said on a public mailing list that the group stopped multi-year campaigns against two Falcon customers [S3].
identification.notes: CrowdStrike name only. No Microsoft Typhoon/Storm name is recorded in this encyclopedia for this actor. Search results for other aggregators (Malpedia, MISP Galaxy) listed it alongside other Chinese-nexus groups, but no cited source here states an alias, so none is added.

attribution.confidence: CrowdStrike describes the group as believed to be of Chinese origin [S1]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Vendor assessment by CrowdStrike. The basis for the China assessment was not visible in the material reviewed.

targeting.notes: CrowdStrike describes the group as targeting infrastructure companies [S1] and in April 2015 described two Falcon customers as affected [S3]. Regions and customer names were not found.

capabilities.summary: CrowdStrike reported use of a 64-bit Windows local privilege-escalation zero-day, CVE-2014-4113, in October 2014 [S1]. Details of initial access and lateral movement tooling previously listed here rested only on an unverified CrowdStrike blog URL and were removed.

gaps: The source (CrowdStrike 'Cyber Deterrence in Action' blog) was removed because its URL did not appear in fact-check search results; claims resting only on it (2013 start, telecom/technology targeting, China Chopper/Mimikatz tradecraft) were removed. Re-add if the URL is verified.
No sponsor, state organization, or government attribution found.
Aliases and overlap with other vendor clusters are unconfirmed; do not merge with Deep Panda, APT19, or others without a cited source.
No activity found after 2015; whether the cluster is still tracked or was merged into a newer CrowdStrike name is unknown.
Dark Reading, SCMP, Malpedia and FireEye coverage of the zero-day surfaced in searches but were not opened or dated, so are not cited.
Specific victims, regions, objectives and infrastructure are not public in the material gathered.

provenance.importedSummary: We have investigated their intrusions since 2013 and have been battling them nonstop over the last year at several large telecommunications and technology companies. The determination of this China-based adversary is truly impressive: they are like a dog with a bone. HURRICANE PANDA's preferred initial vector of compromise and persistence is a China Chopper webshell – a tiny and easily obfuscated 70 byte text file that consists of an ‘eval()’ command, which is then used to provide full command execution and file upload/download capabilities to the attackers. This script is typically uploaded to a web server via a SQL injection or WebDAV vulnerability, which is often trivial to uncover in a company with a large external web presence. Once inside, the adversary immediately moves on to execution of a credential theft tool such as Mimikatz (repacked to avoid AV detection). If they are lucky to have caught an administrator who might be logged into that web server at the time, they will have gained domain administrator credentials and can now roam your network at will via ‘net use’ and ‘wmic’ commands executed through the webshell terminal.
